body:
Different forms of language recognition

India recognises languages for different constitutional, administrative and cultural purposes. Scheduled Language status, official language use and Classical Language status are separate concepts.

A language may belong to more than one category, but inclusion in one category does not automatically confer the others.

The Eighth Schedule

The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages. It is referred to in Articles 344(1) and 351, which concern official language arrangements and the development of Hindi.

The Constitution originally included 14 languages in the Eighth Schedule in 1950.

Expansion of the Eighth Schedule

  • 21st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1967: Added Sindhi, increasing the total to 15.
  • 71st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992: Added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali, increasing the total to 18.
  • 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali, increasing the total to 22. The amendment came into force in 2004.
  • 96th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011: Changed the constitutional name of Oriya to Odia without increasing the number of Scheduled languages.

Scheduled languages by linguistic family

Language groupScheduled languagesCount
Indo-AryanAssamese, Bengali, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Urdu15
DravidianKannada, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu4
AustroasiaticSantali1
Tibeto-BurmanBodo, Manipuri2

As of 26 November 2026, the Eighth Schedule contains these 22 languages.

Scheduled and Classical Languages compared

Of the 11 Classical Languages, 9 are included in the Eighth Schedule: Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Marathi, Assamese and Bengali.

Pali and Prakrit have Classical Language status but are not included in the Eighth Schedule.

Gujarati, Hindi, Punjabi, Urdu and several other languages are included in the Eighth Schedule but do not possess formal Classical Language status at the stated cutoff.

English is not included in the Eighth Schedule. Nevertheless, it continues to be used for official purposes of the Union under the Official Languages Act, 1963.

Official language of the Union

Article 343(1) specifies Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union. It also specifies the international form of Indian numerals for the official purposes of the Union.

The Constitution originally provided for the continued use of English during a transitional period of 15 years from its commencement. Parliament subsequently enacted the Official Languages Act, 1963.

Section 3 of this Act provides for the continued use of English alongside Hindi from 26 January 1965 for all official purposes of the Union for which English was being used immediately before that date and for parliamentary business.

The Constitution does not declare any language to be India's national language. Hindi is the constitutionally designated official language of the Union, and English continues to be used for official purposes under statutory provisions.

Official languages of States

Article 345 permits the legislature of a State to adopt one or more languages in use within that State, or Hindi, for all or selected official purposes of the State, subject to the applicable constitutional provisions.

Therefore, a State's official language need not be the same as the official language of the Union.

Official languages of Gujarat

The Gujarat Official Languages Act, 1960, enacted as Gujarat Act No. 1 of 1961, provides the statutory basis for official language use within Gujarat.

Section 2 identifies Gujarati and Hindi in Devanagari script as languages for official purposes of the State, subject to exceptions and restrictions that the State Government may specify through notifications.

Gujarati is the principal language of Gujarat's regional administration and public life. Its official use is distinct from its inclusion in the Eighth Schedule.

Constitutional protection of linguistic diversity

The Constitution contains provisions intended to protect linguistic identity and accommodate speakers of different languages.

ArticlePrincipal provision
29(1)Right of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it.
30(1)Right of religious and linguistic minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
350Right to submit grievance representations in a language used in the Union or State concerned.
350AEndeavour to provide mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage for children of linguistic minorities.
350BSpecial Officer for linguistic minorities.
351Duty of the Union to promote and develop Hindi.

Article 29(1) applies to any section of Indian citizens possessing a distinct language, script or culture. Its wording does not restrict this conservation right only to minorities.

Articles 350A and 350B were introduced by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956. Article 350A directs States and local authorities to endeavour to provide adequate facilities for primary-stage instruction in the mother tongues of linguistic minority children.

Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for linguistic minorities appointed by the President. The officer investigates matters relating to constitutional safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President.

Mother-tongue education and multilingual learning

The National Education Policy 2020 encourages the use of the home language, mother tongue, local language or regional language as the medium of instruction, wherever possible, until at least Grade 5 and preferably until Grade 8 and beyond.

The policy also supports a flexible three-language formula. It states that no particular language is to be imposed on a State and that at least 2 of the 3 languages selected should be native to India.

These are provisions of an education policy, not an amendment that makes a particular medium of instruction universally compulsory.

Four distinctions for final revision

Gujarati illustrates how a single language can belong to the Indo-Aryan family, use a Brahmi-derived script, appear in the Eighth Schedule and serve official functions in Gujarat, without possessing Classical Language recognition.

Pali illustrates a different combination: it belongs to the Middle Indo-Aryan tradition and has Classical Language recognition, but it is not a Scheduled language.

English illustrates another distinction: a language can serve official functions without being included in the Eighth Schedule or being recognised as a Classical Language.

Prelims focus

  • Eighth Schedule: originally 14 languages; 22 at the stated cutoff.
  • 21st Amendment: Sindhi; 71st Amendment: 3 additions; 92nd Amendment: 4 additions.
  • Pali and Prakrit are Classical Languages outside the Eighth Schedule.
  • Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari as the official language of the Union.
  • Article 350A: mother-tongue instruction for linguistic minority children at the primary stage.
  • Trap: Official language, Scheduled language, Classical Language and national language are not interchangeable terms.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Articles 29, 30, 343–345, 350–351 and Eighth Schedule; Constitution (21st Amendment) Act, 1967; Constitution (71st Amendment) Act, 1992; Constitution (92nd Amendment) Act, 2003; Constitution (96th Amendment) Act, 2011; Official Languages Act, 1963, Section 3; Gujarat Official Languages Act, 1960, Section 2; Ministry of Education, National Education Policy 2020, paragraphs 4.11–4.13; Ministry of Culture, Promotion of Classical Languages, PIB Release ID 2222111, 2 February 2026; Census of India 2011, Language, Paper 1 of 2018, Statement 9. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
